prime.problem: An agent that can write to its own memory can turn one wrong conclusion into an instruction for every later run. If nobody owns the write, a bad memory outlives the transcript that produced it, and nothing tells you where it came from.
prime.fits: The earlier cards in this course showed that the working set is assembled for each turn and that snapshots trade freshness for stability. This card asks what is allowed to persist into those future working sets, and who decides.
prime.goal: Walk any memory write through its four stages, name the evidence that proves each one, and say what goes wrong when two stages are collapsed into one.

attend: Why is an approved Hermes skill still not durable state, and what event actually made it so?
What evidence from the Tuesday run contradicts pytest is flaky, and who should have checked it before the write?
Why does a procedure need a different storage contract from a one-line fact, and what lives in the prompt versus on disk?
Why can a committed memory still be invisible to the session that wrote it?
Which alternative (transcript, vector index, implicit writes) fails on provenance, and which on deletion?

must: Memory is what the system chose to keep → it steers runs long after the source transcript is compacted → a wrong write is a standing instruction → writes are the privileged operation ("writes can corrupt the future")
Approval is a decision, commit is a successful replay through validation → an approved write can still fail (152-char description vs a 60-char budget) → only a changed durable tree proves commit
Sessions load durable state when they start → a commit doesn't reach a running session → activation is proven only by a fresh prompt or an explicit load such as skill_view
Procedures carry ordering, checks and recovery → one memory sentence drops them → store them as skills: a short routing line in the prompt, the body loaded on demand
elevated: Skill routing descriptions sit in every prompt → Hermes caps them at 60 characters → detail must move into the body, and an over-long description fails at replay, not at approval
reference: MEMORY.md (shared facts) and USER.md (user preferences, via memory(target=user)) in Hermes v0.20.1
the exact pending-write fields: source, target, proposal, decision, replay result

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the four stages of a memory write and under each one write the evidence that proves it happened. Then explain in 3–4 sentences why the Tuesday agent's "pytest is flaky" proposal should die at stage 2.
checklist: propose → approve → commit → activate, each a separate event
proof is a file, hash or captured prompt, never the model saying so
approval ≠ commit (replay can fail); commit ≠ activation (needs a new session or load)
the proposal is an agent inference contradicted by two exit-1 runs on the same test
an unreviewed commit would make a false success claim recur in later runs

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between retrieval and memory in terms of what each one owns, and why a vector index alone isn't a memory system.
answer: retrieval brings candidate evidence into a turn (access)
memory decides what persists, for whom, from what source, and when it expires (ownership)
the index finds related text but has no extraction, conflict handling, provenance, TTL, deletion or audit

retrieve.q: Walk the Hermes skill that passed human approval but failed: what happened at each stage, and what finally made it durable?
answer: proposed and staged; the operator approved the diff
replay enforced the 60-character routing-description budget; the 152-character description failed
a 54-character description replayed successfully and committed; a fresh session then loaded it

retrieve.q: You run a coding agent for a team. Which memory writes would you let through without a human, and which would you gate? What does each choice cost?
answer: append-only logs and low-stakes notes: background, no gate, cheap, but noisy
anything that will steer future runs (instructions, procedures, claims about tests) gets a gate
a gate adds latency and reviewer load; no gate risks durable poisoning
the source says most extraction can run off the hot path; the author leaves the boundary as an open question

compare.q: A snapshot freezes what a session sees; a memory commit changes what future sessions see. How does the snapshot explain the "commit ≠ activation" gap, and when would you want a mid-session refresh instead?
answer: the session loaded durable state at start, so later commits are invisible until a new session or a verified refresh
snapshots buy stable, cacheable prompts at the cost of freshness
refresh mid-session only when the user flow needs the write now ("remember this before we continue")
failure modes: snapshot serves stale memory; refresh churns the prompt and breaks caching

compare.q: That card shows skill descriptions as a small line in the prompt prefix. Why does this card treat the same skill as owned state with a lifecycle, and what changes when the agent can write its own skills?
answer: there, skills are installed by a human and only read
here, the agent proposes them, so each one needs source, decision, replay and load evidence
a self-written skill that is wrong is a durable, auto-routed instruction, worse than one bad turn

predict.q: Two Tuesday-style runs, from two different users, both propose "pytest is flaky" for the same repo memory on the same day. One is rejected, one is approved and committed. What does the next fresh session see, and what does the rejection actually protect?
predict.answer: It sees the committed one. Rejection only stops that proposal; it doesn't block equivalent text arriving by another path, and it doesn't erase the transcript or other copies. Shared, project-scoped memory needs dedupe and conflict rules across writers, and the decision has to be about the claim and its evidence, not one proposal object.

apply.done: The "reject flaky" line still prints tree hash 79a7256dc2da (the starting hash, unchanged) even if you now call decide(pid, approve=True), and fresh session sees flaky? stays False.
